extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, regulators, and practitioners in accounting, finance, and corporate governance (SEC/DOJ enforcement, empirical finance scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: An empirical framework for measuring the monetary and reputational costs borne by firms targeted by SEC/DOJ enforcement for financial misrepresentation, using event-study methods and asset- and earnings-based readjustment estimates. The paper defines sample inclusion rules, categorizes announcement events, and describes estimation choices that affect measurement of legal penalties, readjustment (to accurate information), and reputation loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as the expected loss in the present value of future cash flows due to lower sales and higher contracting and financing costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate as the portion of total market value loss that is not explained by the readjustment to accurate financial information or by expected legal penalties. In practice, measure total share-value loss around enforcement-related announcements, estimate and subtract (a) the readjustment effect (market’s repricing to true firm value) and (b) expected legal penalties (SEC/DOJ fines, settlements, and class-action expectations) to obtain reputation loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal penalties (regulatory and judicial monetary sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary fines, civil settlements, and criminal penalties imposed through the legal/regulatory system (SEC, DOJ, courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and sum administrative, civil, and criminal monetary penalties imposed on firms in enforcement actions. Use SEC and DOJ releases, court filings, and settlement records. When estimating total firm loss, include expected legal penalties reflected in market reactions (estimated component) and realized monetary penalties to avoid double counting with charge-offs in asset-based adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readjustment effect (adjustment to accurate financial information)
rubrics_metrics.description: The market’s adjustment to the 'true' firm value when news reveals that previously reported financials were inflated—i.e., change in valuation attributable to correction of misstated assets/earnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate separately from legal penalties and reputation loss. Two main empirical approaches: asset-based (preferred here) and earnings-based. The readjustment is intended to capture correction toward the firm’s value absent the misreporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asset-based method for readjustment effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate the readjustment effect as the product of the firm’s book value of assets written off and the median market-to-book multiple of the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute asset write-offs as the sum of Compustat special items (item #17), accounting changes (item #183), and for banks net charge-offs (item #349). Remove monetary penalties included in charge-offs to avoid double counting. Use contemporaneous two-digit SIC median market-to-book multiples of non-violating firms to convert asset write-offs to estimated market value adjustments. Authors argue this produces more conservative (larger) readjustment estimates than earnings-based in their sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnings-based method for readjustment effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the readjustment by summing restated net income differences (original minus restated) over restated periods and converting to market value using the median industry price-to-earnings multiple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each restated period, multiply the earnings change by the median contemporaneous P/E of the firm’s two-digit SIC industry. Restrict sample to firms with available restatement data (authors restrict to violations beginning after EDGAR phase-in date). Note practical complications: restatement formats vary; some restatements are 'stealth' or incomplete; earnings-based estimates may differ substantially from asset-based estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-study measurement of share-value effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure abnormal returns associated with enforcement-related announcements by subtracting the CRSP value-weighted index return from the firm’s raw return (market-adjusted abnormal returns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors use one-day abnormal returns for trigger and regulatory events, compute parametric t-statistics using the cross-sectional standard error of abnormal returns, and report median results with Mann-Whitney rank tests. Account for overlapping events and multiple event days; report % negative returns. Note that using only surviving (CRSP-listed) firms and single-day windows produces conservative estimates if delisted firms suffered worse outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of announcement/event types
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize events into trigger events (e.g., self-disclosures, restatements, auditor departures, unusual trading), investigation events (firm announcements of informal inquiry or formal investigation), regulatory events (administrative/civil/criminal releases by SEC/DOJ), resolution disclosures, and parallel class-action events (filings and settlements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backfill trigger events from later federal filings when necessary. Distinguish initial disclosure (investigation announcement or regulatory initiation) from resolution disclosures (case resolution releases). Use these categories to attribute abnormal returns to different stages (trigger vs investigation vs regulatory vs resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample universe and inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The universe includes all enforcement actions initiated by the SEC and the DOJ from 1978 through 2002 for violations of 15 USC §§ 78m(b)(2)(A) (books & records), 78m(b)(2)(B) (internal accounting controls), and 78m(b)(5) (circumvention/knowing falsification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors assert this yields the universe of federal enforcement actions for books-and-records and internal-controls financial reporting violations. Use Lexis-Nexis FEDSEC:SECREL, FEDSEC:CASES, SEC website postings, EDGAR, and DOJ records to assemble the sample. Note most enforcement actions also include other charges (fraud, insider trading), and the sample excludes firms that violate but are not caught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of delisted firms and survivorship bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Many target firms are delisted during enforcement periods; returns are only available for surviving (CRSP-listed) firms on specific dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that excluding delisted firms or measuring only specific event-date returns for surviving firms likely understates total valuation losses for the average targeted firm. Authors treat this as a conservative bias and discuss its direction (understatement of reputation loss). Where possible, document delisting incidence and consider its effect on estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and categorization of regulatory events and AAER designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabulate administrative, civil, and criminal events associated with enforcement actions and note secondary AAER (Accounting and Auditing Enforcement Release) designations for SEC releases involving accountants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors count each administrative proceeding/event, civil charge event, and criminal charge event; many occur on same dates so also track unique event days. Record whether SEC releases receive AAER designations; note that AAERs do not capture all enforcement actions involving financial misrepresentation and some enforcement actions lack AAERs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of incomplete/unresolved cases when measuring restatement-based readjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: When using restatement (earnings-based) estimates of readjustment, exclude enforcement actions that are incomplete as of the data cut-off date because restatements often occur at case conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors restrict the earnings-based comparison sample to enforcement actions with violation periods after EDGAR adoption and that were complete by the sample end date to avoid understating restated amounts. This reduces bias where pending cases have not yet restated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of industry median multiples for valuation conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use contemporaneous industry median multiples (two-digit SIC) to convert accounting write-offs or earnings changes into market-value readjustment estimates: median market-to-book for assets, median P/E for earnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute medians from non-violating firms in the same two-digit SIC each year to avoid using firm-specific multiples that are affected by the misreporting. Authors justify market-to-book multiple preference based on literature and empirical performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double counting of penalties in readjustment estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary penalties imposed by regulators or through civil lawsuits may be included in accounting charge-offs; these should be removed when computing asset-based readjustment to avoid double counting with legal penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify monetary penalties within Compustat charge-off items and subtract them before applying the market-to-book multiple. Ensure legal-penalty accounting is not double-counted in both the legal penalties component and the asset-based readjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-sectional analysis of reputation loss determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how reputation loss varies with firm characteristics such as reliance on implicit contracts, financial distress, and debt financing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors test hypotheses from Klein & Leffler and Landes & Posner that reputation loss is larger for firms relying on implicit contracts (e.g., customer relationships) and find positive correlations. Include firm size, industry, and financial condition controls; consider weaker evidence for distress or debt-dependence increasing reputation loss.
